intro: St Anthony preaches to the fish, who enjoy the sermon and change nothing: Mahler turns his song on that story into the Second Symphony’s scherzo. The strings circle tirelessly until the whole orchestra breaks into a cry in B♭ minor.

sections.label: A · Timpani and circling strings
sections.mNote: Timpani sound G and C; the running figures begin

sections.label: B · Bassoons, then a trumpet song
sections.mNote: The middle expands from low phrases to singing brass

sections.label: A′ · The strings circle again
sections.mNote: Short figures return beneath lingering wind and brass notes

sections.label: Coda · Low strings resume their motion
sections.mNote: Held chords fade above restless cellos and basses

cues.title: Two strokes, then circles
cues.text: Timpani strike G and C. The strings start running, with little woodwind comments poking through their uninterrupted figures. The movement’s heading asks for quietly flowing motion; the notes keep turning back on themselves.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, Hofmeister full score (1897), movement III, opening. The dominant–tonic timpani and double ostinato are described at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-3-in-ruhig-fliessender-bewegung-scherzo/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The fish enjoy the sermon
cues.text: In Mahler’s song, St Anthony finds his church empty and takes his sermon to the river. The fish gather with their mouths open. Afterwards the pike still steal and the carp still gorge themselves. They have enjoyed every word.
cues.evidence: The Wunderhorn poem Des Antonius von Padua Fischpredigt, whose music Mahler shares with this scherzo: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/wunderhorn-12/des-knaben-wunderhorn-12-songs-lied-6-des-antonius-von-padua-fischpredigt/

cues.title: The tune sinks lower
cues.text: Bassoons and cellos bring the melody down into the orchestra’s lower voices. The little running figures persist around them. Even when Mahler changes the tune, the water keeps moving.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, p. 86, rehearsal 32: bassoon and cello phrases after the descending orchestral figures. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/e2/IMSLP415748-PMLP49406-GMahler_Symphony_No.2_fe_UE_reprint_RSL1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Eight days between manuscripts
cues.text: On 8 July 1893 Mahler finishes the voice-and-piano manuscript of the fish sermon. Eight days later he dates the scherzo’s orchestral draft. The orchestral song follows on 1 August: song and symphony grow side by side that summer.

cues.title: A trumpet sings
cues.text: A trumpet stretches a long melody over harp arpeggios and running strings. Other trumpets hold soft harmony around it. The brass sounds unexpectedly tender after the woodwinds’ busy gossip.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, p. 100: first-trumpet melody, supporting trumpet parts, harp arpeggios and string figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Back into the current
cues.text: The opening tempo returns. Little figures spread through divided strings while the trumpets hold on above them. The long song drains away, leaving the scherzo’s old restless motion.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, p. 105, rehearsal 43: Zum Tempo I zurückkehren, running string figures and sustained trumpet harmony.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The orchestra cries out
cues.text: The circling scherzo reaches a huge B♭-minor outburst. Brass chords and percussion tower over the running strings. This cry will return at the start of the finale, after the alto’s quiet prayer.
cues.evidence: The B♭-minor climax is described at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-3-in-ruhig-fliessender-bewegung-scherzo/ ; its recall opens movement V, as described on the Foundation’s finale page.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The current starts again
cues.text: Long chords fade in the winds and brass. Underneath, divided cellos and basses resume their quick figures; stopped horns add a pinched, distant sound. The machinery of the scherzo is still turning.
cues.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, p. 118, rehearsal 51: diminuendo, stopped horns and the return of low-string figures.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Bassoons take the lower path
transitions.to: B · Bassoons, then a trumpet song
transitions.how: Descending figures pass down through winds and strings. At rehearsal 32 the bassoons and cellos begin a low, quieter phrase, with horn support and continued movement beneath. The middle section grows from this thinning of the scherzo.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister full score (1897), movement III, p. 86, rehearsal 32.

transitions.title: Held trumpets over returning strings
transitions.from: B · Bassoons, then a trumpet song
transitions.how: Mahler writes Zum Tempo I zurückkehren, returning to the first tempo. Trumpet chords linger while short figures reappear in divided strings, beginning low and spreading upwards. The broad melody releases its hold on the orchestra.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, p. 105, rehearsal 43.

transitions.title: B♭ minor breaks across the dance
transitions.how: Rapid string figures swell into a B♭-minor orchestral outcry. Winds and brass widen into emphatic chords, and percussion reinforces the bass. The running accompaniment is caught inside a much slower, heavier declaration.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, pp. 115–118; B♭-minor climax identified at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-2/symphony-no-2-movement-3-in-ruhig-fliessender-bewegung-scherzo/

transitions.title: Low strings move beneath fading chords
transitions.to: Coda · Low strings resume their motion
transitions.how: The brass and wind chords lengthen and diminish. Stopped horns remain above the quick figures returning in divided cellos and basses. Mahler slows the retreat almost imperceptibly while the lower strings recover the scherzo’s motion.
transitions.evidence: Hofmeister score, movement III, p. 118: Wieder unmerklich zurückhaltend and rehearsal 51, with stopped horns and low-string figures.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 2, full score (Hofmeister 1897; Weinberger/Universal Edition reprint)
source.locator: Third movement, pp. 80–127: opening timpani and strings, trumpet song on p. 100, return at rehearsal 43 and the late orchestral outcry.

timeline.note: Timpani strike G and C before the running figures begin.
Strings circle beneath woodwind interjections; a bundle of twigs strikes the bass drum’s wooden shell.
Bassoons and cellos take the melody into the lower orchestra while the small figures keep moving.
A trumpet sings broadly over harp arpeggios and running strings.
Short string figures return beneath lingering brass and wind notes.
Brass, winds and percussion sound the outcry above the running strings.
Long wind and brass chords fade while cellos and basses resume their quick figures.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
